itens.titulo: If you’re a parent or grandparent, please read this👆
itens.texto:
I've been briefed on things that would empty every grocery store in America if they were made public. I can't share the briefings. But I can share what I've done for my own family since receiving them. And what a retired three-star general started doing quietly every Saturday morning six months ago should tell you more than any headline you've scrolled past this year.

My daughter lives in North Carolina. Married. Two kids. Three states away from me. She calls every Sunday. We talk about the grandkids. About her job. Normal things.

In March I started a different kind of call.

I can't brief her the way I was briefed. I can't show her the files. I can't explain what I know using the words I heard it in. Thirty-one years in uniform and the thing I can't do with what I've learned is SAY it.

But I can tell her what to DO.

So I wrote her a list. Not an emergency checklist from a website. A list from her father. Specific. Ordered. With dates. Each item an instruction I can give without explaining the intelligence behind it.

I mailed it in a plain envelope. No letterhead. No subject line. Just the list. And a note at the top that said: "Do these before September. Don't ask me why on the phone. Just do them. Trust me the way you trusted me when I told you to wear your seatbelt before you understood what a car accident was."

She called me the night she opened it.

"Dad. What is this?"

"A list."

"I can see it's a list. Why does it have DATES on it?"

"Because the things on it need to be done before specific dates. And the most important date is September 30th."

"Why September 30th?"

"I can't tell you why. I can tell you that every person I served with who's been briefed at the level I was briefed has done every item on that list already. Most of them before March."

She was quiet.

"Dad — you're scaring me."

"Good. Scared people prepare. Comfortable people scroll."

Let me show you the list. The same list. Item by item. Because what a three-star general wrote for his daughter is what I'd write for every family in this country if I could mail it to 100 million houses.

ITEM 1: Find every freshwater source within two miles of your house. Creek. Pond. Stream. Rain collection point. Map them. Walk to each one. Measure the distance. Time the walk.

She called about this one first.

"Why do I need to know where the creeks are?"

"Because someday the thing you turn on in your kitchen every morning might not give you what it's supposed to. And when that day comes — the answer isn't in your garage. It's in the landscape around your house that you've driven past for twelve years without thinking about."

"When is 'someday'?"

"The list has a date on it."

"But Dad — we have food. Flashlights. Batteries. Generator. We're prepared."

"You're prepared for everything that LASTS. Food lasts months. Batteries last years. Generator fuel — you can fill a tank. First aid sits in a cabinet. You can stockpile almost everything your family needs."

"There is ONE thing you cannot stockpile enough of. The one thing your body can't go three days without. A case lasts less than a day for your family. A garage full — maybe two weeks if you ration so hard the kids cry. Then it's over. Every bottle opened is one fewer. Storage isn't a plan. It's a countdown. And the scenarios I've been briefed on outlast every countdown you can fit in your garage."

"That's what Item 2 solves. Not with more storage. With ACCESS. A source that doesn't count down."

ITEM 2: Get a gravity-fed filtration system. Guard Survival. Veteran-owned. 0.1-micron membrane. Keep it under your sink. Test it at the nearest creek. Learn how to fill it, hang it, open the valve. Do it BEFORE you need it. Do it ten times before you need it once.

She Googled it. Called me back.

"It's a water filter, Dad."

"It's a water INDEPENDENCE system. It disconnects your family from every vulnerability on every other item on this list. The faucet needs a grid needs fuel needs a strait needs a government needs a law that expires on September 30th. This needs a creek and gravity."

"Fifteen hundred gallons per filter. That's four months for your family. The creek behind Jackson's school — I looked it up from my desk. Seven-minute walk from your front door."

She was quiet again.

"You looked up the creek near my son's school?"

"I looked up the creek near my son's school. My daughter's school. My neighbor's church. Every person I love — I've mapped the source closest to them. Because that's what you do when you've read what I've read. You find the source that doesn't connect to anything in the file."

ITEM 3: Fill both bathtubs the moment you hear the word "advisory" on any channel. Don't wait for confirmation. Don't wait for details. Fill first. Ask questions later.

"Why the bathtubs?"

"Because the window between an advisory being issued and the pressure dropping is measured in hours. Sometimes minutes. The bathtub is the one container in your house that holds enough to buy time. Fill it BEFORE the pressure drops. Once it drops you've lost the reservoir."

ITEM 4: Do NOT depend on bottled water as your primary plan. Cases are a countdown. Every bottle opened is one fewer. A case lasts less than a day for a family of four. Your garage is not a solution. It's a timer.

"But we have cases in the garage."

"How many?"

"Six."

"That's four days. Maybe five. The scenarios I've been briefed on don't resolve in four days. They resolve in weeks. Sometimes months. Your six cases give you until Wednesday. Wednesday through whenever is the gap the list is designed to fill."

"Dad. What scenarios?"

"I can't tell you the scenarios. I can tell you the list fills the gap the scenarios create. Do the list. The list is the answer to questions I can't say out loud."

ITEM 5: Test the system before you need it. Go to the creek on a Saturday. Fill the bag. Hang it. Open the valve. Watch what happens. Bring the kids. Make it normal. Because the first time you need it should NOT be the first time you use it.

She did it. Last Saturday. She sent me a photo. Brown water in the bag. Clear water in the jug. Jackson standing next to it looking curious. Her husband standing behind him looking like he was watching something he didn't fully understand yet.

She texted me one line under the photo: "It works. Jackson thinks it's a science experiment."

I texted back: "Let him think that."

Because he's six. He doesn't need to know what Grandpa read in a room he'll never see. He needs to know where the creek is and how the bag works. The rest is for his mother and his father. And the list.

ITEM 6: Do all of this before September 30th. Not most of it. ALL of it. The date matters. I can't tell you why the date matters. But every person I served with — every person who's read what I've read — has September 30th circled. Not as a prediction. As a DEADLINE. The kind of deadline that doesn't move because you're not ready for it.

She's done. Every item. Three states away. Her family is set up. The creek mapped. The system tested. The bathtubs ready. The cases understood as a timer, not a plan.

She called me last Sunday. Normal call. Grandkids. Her job. Then at the end:

"Dad — thank you for the list."

"You don't need to thank me."

"I know you can't tell me everything. But the list tells me enough. Because my father doesn't write lists like this for no reason. And the fact that you wrote it — with dates — tells me more than the news ever could."

She's right. I can't share the briefing. I can't show you the file. I can't say the words I heard them in.

But I can give you the same list I gave her.

https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1

Item 2 is the one that matters most. The source that doesn't connect to anything in the briefing. The filter that doesn't need the grid or the fuel or the strait or the law or the date. The creek your family has been driving past for years that becomes the most important thing on your property the morning the faucet stops giving you what it's supposed to.

https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1

A three-star general with thirty-one years of service and briefings you'll never see wrote a list for his daughter with dates on it. Every person he served with has done the same items. The list is the briefing translated into action. September 30th is on it. And the one item that changes everything is the one that disconnects your family from every system in the file.

Here's the one on my list:

https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1

EDIT: Since I mailed the list my daughter has given copies to three families on her street. No explanation. Just the list. The same way I gave it to her — do it before September. Don't ask why. Guard Survival is a small veteran-owned operation — limited stock. The list is circulating. The date isn't moving.

P.S. — Proverbs 27:12 — "The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty." The list is the refuge. September 30th is the danger. Every item on it was written by a man who's read what the danger looks like in words you'll never hear. Do the list. Before the date. Here's the one I got for ours: 🙏

https://guardsurvival.com/products/aqua-gs1

itens.titulo: If you’re a parent or grandparent, please read this👆
itens.texto:
The great blackout is coming. The people at the top have known for months, and as of this morning, they've stopped acting like they don't. I've been in the Army for over 30 years. Two hours ago I walked out of a briefing where they told us Operation FORTRESS is now active. 

I can't tell you who told me, or what comes next. But I can show you how I protected my own family before I even drove home. And the general who ran that room moved his grandkids out of the city last weekend.

I almost didn't post this. If my name ever gets tied to it, I could lose a pension I spent 30 years earning.

But I'm not writing this as a colonel. I'm writing it as a husband, a dad, and a son.

My name is Dan. I'm 56, and my wife Susan and I live outside San Antonio. Our daughter Katie lives twenty minutes away with two little boys, Wyatt and Cole, who think I hung the moon. My mom is 84 and lives alone in Kerrville, and she still won't let anyone help her carry the groceries.

We're a normal family. Church on Sunday, and a dog who's scared of thunder.

So let me tell you what I can.

On September 30th, the Secretary of War signed a memo called FORTRESS. You can look it up.

It says every major base in this country has to be able to run for 90 days with no help from the outside world. Its own power, its own fuel, its own phones.

And its own WATER.

Count 90 days from the day it was signed, and you land on December 29th. That's the date every base is getting ready for. When the blackout comes, they plan to be ready. And that clock is running out.

And it's not just us. Britain just told its families to stock up on food and water. When a government tells its own people to get ready, it's not because it plans to come help them.

I've sat in a lot of briefings, and most of them are boring. Slides, coffee, and men checking their watches.

This morning's wasn't boring.

We locked our phones in little steel boxes outside the door, and nobody checked a watch the whole time.

For the first time in all the years I've sat in rooms like that, nobody said "if." Every single person said "when."

You've seen the news. Tucker Carlson wrote that the call on a nuclear strike on Iran could come very soon, and a former CIA officer said the same thing on TV the next night.

I can't tell you if they're right. I can tell you nobody in that room laughed.

When it was over, the general who ran the room packed up his folder and left without his usual jokes. I found out later what he did last weekend.

He drove his daughter's kids out to his brother's ranch in the Hill Country, and he didn't drive them back.

But this morning wasn't my first FORTRESS briefing. The first one was three weeks ago, and that's the one that changed what I did for my family. So that's the one I need to tell you about.

Here's the part I can tell you, because none of it is secret. It's what they're building.

Power, they can buy. Small reactors, big batteries, and their own little grid that can cut loose from yours with one switch. The man from the Pentagon said it plain: "Power is combat now."

Then we got to water.

Power got twelve slides. Water got one.

And the man who ran it said, "Pumps need power. So we stop counting on pumps."

The answer on that slide wasn't a tank or a truck. It was the river, and gravity.

The water team lead in that room was a master sergeant with twenty-two years in. Quiet guy. I caught him in the hall and asked, "What do you keep at your house?"

He pulled out his phone and showed me a picture of his garage. There was a gray bag hanging on a hook by the door, and that was it.

"Go home and count your water, sir," he said. "Then you'll get it."

When a master sergeant says that, you listen. I ordered three of whatever that bag was from my truck, before I even left the parking lot.

Then I sat there for a while and thought about February 2021.

I was running a base here in Texas when the grid went down. Our lights stayed on, our generators kicked in, and our people had hot coffee.

And three miles outside our gate, families were melting snow in soup pots.

Millions of Texans got told to boil their water that week, and a lot of them had no power to boil it with. I watched it from behind a fence, and I never forgot it.

So when I got home that night, I did what he said and went straight to the garage.

Susan followed me out. "What are you doing?"

"Counting."

We had six cases of the little bottles stacked by the freezer. I'd bought them after 2021 and felt pretty good about it.

Six cases is about 19 gallons. For Susan, me and the dog, with drinking, cooking and washing up, that's about a week if we're careful.

FORTRESS plans for 90 days.

I stood there with a case in my hands and felt sick.

Keep your cases. I still have mine. But do the math on them, because stored water is a countdown. Every bottle you drink is one less bottle.

And here's what most people don't know, because nobody ever tells them.

Your tap doesn't run on water. It runs on power.

The power runs the pumps. The pumps make the pressure. And the pressure pushes the water to your sink.

Lose the power, and the pressure starts to drop. Not in weeks.

Hours.

And they don't even need a bomb to do it. This July, the FBI warned that hackers had gone after town water systems in seven states in one week. Minnesota alone had more than 30 hit.

I thought about Wyatt. He's four, and he doesn't know what a boil notice is. He just knows how to walk up to me and say, "Papa, I'm thirsty."

And I thought about what happens on day eight, when the cases are gone.

I've seen it. You get in a line at the high school gym, show your ID, take your two jugs, and come back tomorrow to do it again. You go where they tell you, and you wait as long as they say.

Nobody has to make you. Thirst does it for them.

That's the part of the plan nobody puts on a slide.

When the switch flips, the gate closes and the bases keep going. Your family is on the other side of that fence, standing in that line.

Mine too, if I let it happen.

So I stopped counting bottles and started thinking about sources.

There's a creek we cross every Sunday on the way to church, Salado Creek. Susan's driven over it a thousand times, and it's never once been dry.

Most people are surrounded by water they can't use.

I had two of those filter straws in the truck. Good. Keep them. But a straw helps one person drink, bent over a creek. Families need gallons, not sips.

The men in that room don't count bottles. They count sources.

That's when I got it. That gray bag.

I called the master sergeant back. "It's a gravity filter."

She was quiet again.

"I looked up the creek near my son's school. My daughter's school. My neighbor's church. Every person I love — I've mapped the source closest to them. Because that's what you do when you've read what I've read. You find the source that doesn't connect to anything in the file."

ITEM 3: Fill both bathtubs the moment you hear the word "advisory" on any channel. Don't wait for confirmation. Don't wait for details. Fill first. Ask questions later.

"Why the bathtubs?"

"Because the window between an advisory being issued and the pressure dropping is measured in hours. Sometimes minutes. The bathtub is the one container in your house that holds enough to buy time. Fill it BEFORE the pressure drops. Once it drops you've lost the reservoir."

ITEM 4: Do NOT depend on bottled water as your primary plan. Cases are a countdown. Every bottle opened is one fewer. A case lasts less than a day for a family of four. Your garage is not a solution. It's a timer.

"But we have cases in the garage."

"How many?"

"Six."

"That's four days. Maybe five. The scenarios I've been briefed on don't resolve in four days. They resolve in weeks. Sometimes months. Your six cases give you until Wednesday. Wednesday through whenever is the gap the list is designed to fill."

"Dad. What scenarios?"

"I can't tell you the scenarios. I can tell you the list fills the gap the scenarios create. Do the list. The list is the answer to questions I can't say out loud."

ITEM 5: Test the system before you need it. Go to the creek on a Saturday. Fill the bag. Hang it. Open the valve. Watch what happens. Bring the kids. Make it normal. Because the first time you need it should NOT be the first time you use it.

She did it. Last Saturday. She sent me a photo. Brown water in the bag. Clear water in the jug. Owen standing next to it looking curious. Her husband standing behind him looking like he was watching something he didn't fully understand yet.

She texted me one line under the photo: "It works. Owen thinks it's a science experiment."

I texted back: "Let him think that."

Because he's six. He doesn't need to know what Grandpa read in a room he'll never see. He needs to know where the creek is and how the bag works. The rest is for his mother and his father. And the list.

ITEM 6: Do all of this before Thanksgiving. Not most of it. ALL of it. Before everyone you love sits down at one table, under your roof. The date matters. I can't tell you why the date matters. But every person I served with — every person who's read what I've read — has Thanksgiving week circled. Not as a prediction. As a DEADLINE. The kind of deadline that doesn't move because you're not ready for it.

She's done. Every item. Three states away. Her family is set up. The creek mapped. The system tested. The bathtubs ready. The cases understood as a timer, not a plan.

She called me last Sunday. Normal call. Grandkids. Her job. Then at the end:

"Dad — thank you for the list."

"You don't need to thank me."

"I know you can't tell me everything. But the list tells me enough. Because my father doesn't write lists like this for no reason. And the fact that you wrote it — with dates — tells me more than the news ever could."

She's right. I can't share the briefing. I can't show you the file. I can't say the words I heard them in.

But I can give you the same list I gave her.

itens.titulo: If you're a parent or grandparent, please read this👆
itens.texto:
My neighbor got home from work on a Tuesday in June and started emptying his savings account. Not all at once. A little every few days, the way you would if you didn't want anyone asking. He sold the boat. He told his daughter she wasn't going back to school in the fall. His wife thought he was leaving her. He told me the real reason over the fence on a Sunday morning and I have not slept properly since. That was six weeks ago. I still haven't told my son. But I've already done every single thing he said.

His name is Ray.

Sixty-one. Runs the overnight crew at a plant two counties over. Twenty-six years there.

The dullest man on this street and I mean that kindly.

We've lived beside Ray and Denise since 2011. Fourteen years. He mows in straight lines. He waves with two fingers off the wheel. In fourteen years I have never heard that man raise his voice about anything, including the time my dog got into his tomatoes.

Which is why I noticed.

It started with the boat.

That boat sat on his driveway for nine years. He was never going to use it and we all knew it and it was a running joke on this street. In June it was gone in four days.

Then Katie didn't go back to school.

Then Denise called me on a Thursday morning crying.

"He's taking money out of the bank. Cash. He won't say what for."

I said something useless. I think I said men get funny at that age.

"I think he's got somebody," she said.

I didn't believe that for a second. But I didn't have anything better.

Then on Sunday morning I looked out of my kitchen window and saw Ray doing something I had never once seen him do in fourteen years.

He was digging.

Not gardening. Digging. Shovel, boots, a pile of dirt beside the shed, hole already past his knee.

Ray pays a boy to do the heavy yard work. Ray does not dig.

He'd been at it about an hour. No radio. No water bottle. Just digging.

I watched him for a while from the sink. Then I poured two coffees and walked out to the fence.

"Ray."

He looked up.

"I brought you a coffee."

He put the shovel down and came over. Wiped his forehead with his sleeve.

"Thank you."

"Ray, what in the world are you doing back there?"

"Putting some things away."

"Away."

"That's right."

"In a hole."

"That's right."

I laughed a little. He didn't.

"Denise called me Thursday. She was crying."

That got him. He looked down into his coffee.

"I know she did. She told me."

"She thinks you're leaving her."

"I know."

"So what are you actually doing?"

He didn't answer right away. He looked off past his shed at the tree line.

I waited. I'm good at waiting.

"You know I can't really talk about work."

"I'm not asking you about work."

"Everything I'd tell you right now is work."

I didn't say anything to that.

"There've been a lot of meetings this spring," he said. "That's all it is."

"All right."

"Some of them have been hard to sit through."

So I tried it another way.

"Ray. What are you getting ready for?"

That one was different. He took a long breath in through his nose.

"You watching the news? The shipping lane?"

"The Strait. Everybody is. You can't fill a tank any more without wincing."

He nodded, slow.

"That's the part they're letting you see."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning the price of gas is the surface. The meetings I've been sitting in are about what gets decided because of the price of gas. And that part isn't on the news yet."

"What part?"

He was quiet a second.

Then he said, "You remember 2020?"

"Which bit?"

"The bit where somebody else decided which stores you were allowed to walk into. How far you could drive. How many people could sit in your own living room."

"I remember."

"They did it once and it worked. They know how now."

I felt something go cold across my chest.

"They know how to do what?"

"Same thing. They'll just give you a different reason for it."

"Ray."

"Fuel first. Cards, limits per household per week, you prove you've got somewhere worth going. Hospitals get theirs, trucking gets theirs, everybody else waits in line."

"That doesn't happen here."

"It's happening somewhere else right now. It just hasn't gotten here yet."

"All right."

"Then it's power. An hour here, three hours there. Please don't run your dryer between two and seven. And you'll do it, because what else are you going to do."

"Ray, stop."

"I'm not trying to frighten you."

"You're doing a heck of a job anyway."

He almost smiled at that. Almost.

"So what do I do?" I said. "Buy a generator? Fill the pantry?"

And he laughed. A tired little laugh, not a real one.

"Everything you just said. The pantry. The cash. The boat. Katie coming home. All of that is the easy part."

"Easy."

"That's what anybody who's lived through a real shortage would tell you to do. Anybody over eighty who remembers the seventies. Anybody in my line of work who's been watching this build since March. That's not insight. That's just homework."

"Ray, you are burying money in your backyard. That is not homework."

"It is to the people who know."

I let that sit.

"So then what is it," I said. "What's the thing keeping you up?"

He turned the coffee cup around in his hands.

"It's something I worked out sitting in a meeting I probably shouldn't have been in. Nobody outside that room is saying it out loud yet. And I'd trade everything in that hole for it if somebody made me choose."

"Ray."

He looked at me.

"Water."

"Water?"

"When this lands, water is the thing. Not gas. Not cash. Not what's in your freezer."

"Water."

"You can go a long time without food. You can go a good while cold. You cannot go long at all without clean water, and the second every household in this country works that out on the same afternoon, it's over."

"Over how?"

"The water aisle goes first. Then Costco. After that there's no water for sale anywhere at any price. You're drinking what you put back or you're not drinking."

"But the tap."

"The tap's the part nobody sees coming."

"The tap's fine."

"The tap is a supply chain. It's power, and it's chemicals that arrive on a truck, and the truck runs on the diesel we were just talking about. Every step between the river and your kitchen has somebody else's problem in it. When one of them wobbles, you get a notice telling you to boil your water."

"So you boil it."

"On what?"

I didn't have an answer for that.

"If the reason the water's bad is the power," he said, "then your stove's out too. So now you're boiling water on a grill in the yard with whatever propane's in the tank. For how long? Three days? Three weeks?"

I said, all right, but how often does that actually happen. And I expected him to have a number ready, because Ray always has a number ready.

He shook his head.

"I'm not giving you a number."

"Why not?"

"Because you'd take my word for it. And you shouldn't take anybody's word for it, including mine, including whoever's selling you something next week."

"Ray."

"Go inside. Type in your own county and the words boil advisory. Not the state. Your county. Then read what comes up and make your own mind up."

So I did. That evening, at my own kitchen table, on my own laptop.

I'm not going to tell you what I found, because you should go and do exactly what I did. It took me four minutes.

I'll only say I stopped thinking he was having a breakdown.

Here's the part I actually sat down to write about, though. Because the fuel and the hole in the yard is not why I'm typing this at eleven at night.

The following Sunday I went back out to the fence and asked him whether I should be buying water.

He said something I wasn't expecting.

"Water you store is a number that only goes down."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning you can stack that garage to the roof and all you've bought is a countdown. Two weeks. Four if you're careful and you stop washing. Then it's gone, and the tap is still bad, and there's no truck coming."

"So what do you do instead?"

"You quit storing water and you get something that makes it."

Now I'll be straight with you. Standing there I was sure a sales pitch was coming. Forty years of church suppers and school fundraisers teaches you to hear one coming. People go slightly polite right before they want something off you.

It didn't come.

He said "hold on," went in through his back door and came out with something in his fist.

Held it up.

"This."

"That's a pen."

"It's a filter. You drink through it. Or you screw it onto a bottle."

"Ray, that's nothing. That's the size of a marker."

"That's the point of it. It goes in a drawer. It doesn't want power. It doesn't want a refill. And it doesn't go off sitting there."

"And that works?"

"You're going to ask me that again in about four minutes. Put your shoes on."

There's a creek behind our houses. There's been a creek behind these houses since before either of us moved in. It runs down past the back of the Hendersons' place toward the culvert. It is brown. There is a tire in it. Nobody has ever thought about that creek for one second in their life.

He crouched down at the edge and filled an empty bottle straight out of it.

I want you to understand what that water looked like. Not tea-colored. Brown. There were things turning over in it. I would not have washed a car with it.

He screwed the little tube onto the neck of the bottle and squeezed some out into a mug I'd carried down with me.

What came out was clear.

Then he drank some. Standing in the mud in his Sunday shoes, in front of me.

Then he held it out.

"You first," I said.

"I just went first."

So I drank it.

I'm going to be careful here because I don't want to sell you something I didn't get. It tasted like water. That's all. Regular water, cold because the creek was cold. There was no grit in it. It didn't smell like anything. There was nothing about it that made me want to spit it out on his shoes.

I pulled the bottle back and looked at it.

The water in the bottle was still brown.

What had come through was clear.

I said something I won't write down.

He turned it over and told me how it works, and I wrote this down when I got home because I wanted to get it right and because I knew nobody would believe me otherwise.

There are two parts to it. The first part is the straining. He gave me the number, a hundredth of a micron, and that meant nothing to me standing in a creek. What it means in plain words is it catches the bacteria and the muck.

The second part is the one he said nobody talks about, and it's carbon. Carbon is what pulls out the chemicals and the taste.

"The first part is why it's safe," he said. "The second part is why a child will actually drink it. Most of the cheap ones only do the first part. So it's technically safe and it tastes like the bottom of a pond, and then your grandbaby won't touch it, and you're right back where you started with a screaming child and no water."

That was the sentence that got me. Not the micron. That one.

I asked how long one lasts.

Eighteen hundred gallons. And it doesn't expire sitting on a shelf, which is more than I can say for the case of water in my basement with 2019 on the side of it.

"Buy it once," he said. "Put it in a drawer. Forget about it until the day you can't."

He put the one from his hand into mine.

"Take that. I've got more. I'll bring some over tomorrow. Give them to your kids. Don't make a production of it. They don't need to understand it. They just need to have one when it matters."

Then he went back to his hole.

Here's what I did about it.

I walked back up from the creek, got in my car to go to the store, and then sat in it on my own driveway for about ten minutes without starting it, if you want the truth.

Because nobody tells you what it's like to be the one who finds out first. My son Marcus is forty minutes away. My daughter is two states over. There are eleven houses on this street and I know every person in nine of them. Nancy across the street is eighty-three and she has nobody.

And I sat there doing arithmetic in my head about how many I could afford. Not how many I needed. How many I could afford.

I'm seventy-two. Bill is seventy-five. We are not people with money. Every dime counts in this house and has since he retired.

And I remember thinking, very clearly: I do not have enough water to help this whole street.

Ray dropped a bag on my porch Monday morning. Didn't knock. Just left it.

I drove to Marcus's on Tuesday and gave him three. One for him, one for Amy, one for the truck.

I mailed two to my daughter with a note that said don't argue with me.

I walked one across to Nancy and told her it was a spare.

My son-in-law rolled his eyes at me. I watched him do it, right across the kitchen table.

I don't care. He can roll his eyes.

Denise has stopped worrying about Ray, by the way. She keeps one in her purse now.

Now listen. I'm not going to sit here and tell you the world is ending. Ray never said that, and I'm not going to say it on his behalf.

What he said is that there are more moving parts between the river and your kitchen tap than anybody realizes, and when one of them stops, the entire plan is a piece of paper telling you to boil water you have no way of boiling.

That's it. That's the whole thing.

If you've had a feeling these last few weeks that something is off, and the news keeps going around it without landing on it, you're not making that up and you're not being dramatic.

The people who know are getting ready. Quietly. They're not making announcements.

This is the one Ray put in my hand over that fence. I've put the link underneath.

👉 tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial

EDITED TO ADD:

I did not expect this to go anywhere. It has not stopped since Thursday.

Two ladies from my Tuesday group. My cousin in Ohio. A woman I have not spoken to since Bill's surgery. All asking me the same thing, which is where do I get one.

The link is up above and it's the only place I know of. It isn't in the stores here. I checked two of them before I ever went out to that fence, which tells you how much attention I was paying.

Don't take my word for any of it, by the way. Go and read what it does. I didn't take Ray's word for it either, and he's the one who handed it to me.

I'd rather tell you that than have you find out later I'd dressed something up.

P.S. I finally told Marcus the whole thing, start to finish. Including the part about the grill. He listened the whole way through without saying a word, which is not like him. When I finished he asked me one question. "How far's the nearest water from you?" I'd already worked it out. Four hundred yards, the creek. He didn't ask anything else, and two days later Amy texted me a photo of theirs in the glovebox.

P.P.S. I asked Ray what he'd say to somebody who thinks all this is a bit much. He said: "Ask them what their plan is. Not what they're worried about. Their plan." I've asked four people that now. Nobody's had one. I didn't have one either, six weeks ago.

P.P.P.S. One of them does eighteen hundred gallons. I had to look up what that meant. It's years, for one person, out of a creek or a rain barrel or the tub you filled the night before. Nothing to plug in and nothing to replace. That's the part I'd want somebody to tell me.

P.P.P.P.S. And if you're sitting there thinking you'll just buy the jugs instead, go back and read what Ray said about the countdown. Stored water runs out. That isn't a criticism of storing water, I've got a basement full of it, it's just arithmetic. Being able to make water safe does not run out. Fourteen years of knowing a man and it took him ten minutes in a creek to explain the difference to me.

👉 tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial

itens.titulo: If you have kids or grandkids, please take five minutes and read this👆
itens.texto:
My neighbor's husband came home from a work trip to Washington last month and started quietly shutting his family's life down. Sold the bass boat he spent six years fixing up. Cancelled the Alaska cruise for their 35th anniversary. Moved money out of the bank. Talked his son into hauling the grandkids back from Phoenix. His wife was sure a doctor had given him bad news and he was hiding it from her. He told me the real reason over our back fence, and it came down to one word. That was three weeks ago. I still haven't told my husband. But I've quietly done every single thing he told me to do, before the rest of this street figures it out.

His name is Warren.

61 years old. Thirty-four years in fuel logistics. The steadiest man I know.

I've lived next door to Warren and Marlene for 14 years. Our grandkids run through the same sprinkler.

Warren leaves Monday and comes home Thursday. Houston mostly. This year, a lot of Washington.

Doesn't say much. Waves from the mower. You ask him something, you get the answer and nothing extra.

In 14 years I have not once seen that man rattled.

So when he started acting odd in August, I noticed.

First it was the boat.

Then the cruise. Marlene had that brochure on her fridge since Christmas.

Then the bank. She found the withdrawal slips in his jacket pocket.

Then a moving truck pulled in from Phoenix. Their son Kyle, his wife, two little girls and the dog. Into the basement "for a while." Nobody would tell her why.

Then the deliveries started. Plain brown boxes. A whole pallet one time. Straight into his shop with the door pulled shut behind him.

Marlene sat at my kitchen table on a Wednesday and cried.

"He's sick. I know he's sick. He got some kind of news and he's putting his affairs in order and he won't tell me."

I didn't know what to say to her.

Then Saturday morning I was at the sink, looked out my kitchen window, and saw Warren doing something I have never seen him do in 14 years.

He was splitting firewood.

Two cords at least, dumped beside his shop. Warren out there in his work shirt with a maul, swinging.

Warren and Marlene have gas logs. They've had gas logs since the day they moved in.

He'd been at it better than an hour. No radio. No gloves. Just swinging.

I stood there and watched him a good 20 minutes.

Then I poured two coffees and walked out to the fence.

"Warren."

He stopped.

"Brought you a coffee."

He looked at the maul. Looked at the pile. Looked at me.

Then he leaned the maul on the stump and came over.

"Thank you."

"Warren, what on earth are you doing?"

"Getting some wood in."

"Wood."

"Yep."

"For the gas logs."

"Wood stove's coming Thursday."

I laughed. He didn't.

"Warren. Come on now."

"It's a stove. People have stoves. It's no big thing."

"A box of candles is no big thing. You've got a lumber yard back there."

I nearly got a smile out of him.

"Marlene thinks I've gone off the deep end."

"Marlene thinks you're dying. She sat at my table Wednesday and cried about it."

That one got to him. He looked down in his cup.

"I know. She asked me straight out that night."

"She thinks you've got six months and you won't tell her, Warren."

"I know."

"So what is it really."

Nothing. He drank some coffee. Looked off past his shop at the tree line.

I waited.

"You know I can't talk about work."

"I didn't ask about work."

"Anything I've got to say right now is work."

I kept my mouth shut.

"I've sat in a lot of rooms since the spring. That's all it is."

"All right."

"A few of them I'd have paid good money not to be in."

I came at it another way.

"Warren. What are you getting ready for?"

That one he felt.

He let out a long breath.

"You been following the oil thing? The strait?"

"Hormuz. Sure. Gas is ridiculous again. It's all anybody talks about after church."

He nodded slow.

"That's the piece you're allowed to watch."

"Meaning what."

"Meaning the news shows you the ships. The rooms I've been in aren't about ships. They're about what gets done here, at home, once fuel gets short enough. None of that's been on your TV."

"What gets done."

He went quiet again.

Then: "You remember 2020?"

"Which part."

"The part where somebody decided which stores were essential. Where they told you how many people could sit at your own table at Thanksgiving. Where two weeks turned into a year."

"I remember."

"Well, they kept the binder. All of that got built once and nobody took it apart."

I went cold right down both arms.

"Kept it for what."

"For this. Same binder. New reason."

"Warren."

"Fuel goes first. They won't call it rationing, they'll call it a conservation order. So many gallons per household per week. Odd and even days by your license plate. Military and hospitals fill up first, then farms, then trucking. You and me get what's left and a line to stand in."

"That doesn't happen in America."

"It did happen in America. 1973. You and I are both old enough to remember our dads sitting in those lines. And it's happening right now. Slovenia started rationing gas in March. Fifty liters a day. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency that same week. We're not at the front of the line. But we're in it."

"Okay."

"Then trucking. Diesel goes where they say it goes. Store shelves get thin, then patchy. Flights get cut and they'll blame prices."

"Okay."

"Then the power. Plants get told to throttle back. Brownouts. An hour. Then an afternoon. Kindly don't run your air conditioner between two and seven."

"Warren."

"And 2020 had an end because a virus runs its course. This one runs until the oil moves. They signed a deal in June and it was dead in three days. The truce fell apart in July. The Navy's cleared better than a hundred suspected mines out of that water and the ships still won't go. There's one pipeline across Saudi Arabia that gets oil around the strait. One side door, and everything is leaning on it. Nobody in those rooms is talking in weeks."

I just stood there.

"That's why Kyle and the girls are in my basement. That's why the boat's gone. That's why there's a stove coming Thursday."

"All right. So what do I do?"

He looked at me a while. Then he sort of laughed. A worn out laugh.

"Tell you the truth, everything I just listed is the easy part."

"Easy?"

"It's what your grandmother would've done without anybody telling her. Anybody who sat in a gas line in '73. None of it takes inside knowledge. It's chores."

"You sold a boat you loved, Warren. Don't stand there and tell me that's chores."

"It is to the people who know."

I didn't answer him.

"None of that is what has me up at three in the morning."

"Then what does."

Long drink of coffee.

"Something that came up about a month in. One slide, in a room I only got into because somebody was out sick. They spent four minutes on it and went on. I'd give up every box in that shop before I'd give up my answer to it."

"Your answer to what?"

He looked right at me.

"Water."

"Water?"

"When this gets bad, clean water is the whole ballgame. Ahead of cash. Ahead of a full tank. Ahead of that wood pile."

"Water."

"You can be hungry a good while. You can get through a cold house with blankets. You get about three days without water. And the day every household in the country works that out at the same time, it's done."

"Done how."

"Austin, Texas, 2018. One boil notice. The stores were out of bottled water in hours. Hours. And that was one city, with the trucks all running and the rest of the country to pull from. Now do every city at once with diesel on a conservation order."

"But we've got the tap."

"The tap goes too. Nobody ever sees that one coming."

"Warren."

"Water gets to your house because electric pumps push it there. Pumps lose power, the pressure drops, and when the pressure drops, whatever's in the ground around those old pipes can get pulled inside them. That's why they tell you to boil. I didn't make that up, it's in the EPA's own guidance."

"Texas, February 2021. Grid went down in the cold. Over fourteen million people had their water knocked out or messed up. Some of the boil notices ran past a month. The man who ran the state's own environmental agency told a reporter he was on day four with no water at his house. Him, his family, his dog and eight chickens."

"Fourteen million."

"Fourteen million. From a cold snap. Asheville after the hurricane, fifty-three days before they could drink from the tap. Jackson, Mississippi, close to seven weeks. Richmond, Virginia, January of last year. One power outage at the water plant and the whole city was boiling water."

"Every one of those was weather. One place at a time. With the whole rest of the country standing by to send trucks."

"What I'm telling you about is everywhere at once. And nobody's standing by, because everybody's in it."

He set his cup on the fence post.

"Picture it. Your grandbabies are thirsty. The store's empty. The tap's running brown, or it isn't running. There's no truck coming because the truck has no diesel. And you're stood in your kitchen trying to work out what goes in the sippy cup."

"Don't."

"I know. I'm sorry. But that's the one that gets me up at night. Everybody's staring at the gas pump. Nobody's looking at the faucet."

"This can't be right."

"Ask yourself why every headline says oil and not one of them says water. The folks in those rooms know how this goes. They won't say it out loud, because the minute they do, the water aisle is empty by supper. That's what 'avoiding a panic' means."

"All right. So what are you doing about it?"

He looked at his cup.

"We're covered."

"What's that mean."

"Means we're covered."

"Warren."

"I'd rather leave it there."

"You haven't left one thing there in twenty minutes."

Nothing.

"Warren. You just stood my granddaughter in my kitchen with an empty sippy cup. You do not get to say that to me and go back to chopping wood."

He looked at me a long moment.

"It's not something I'm meant to be passing around."

"Passing what around."

"What people in my line of work are doing at their own houses."

"Tell me."

He sighed. Looked at the shop. Looked at the wood. Looked back at me.

"There's an item. One particular item. Everybody I trust in this business has them. The fella who runs our Gulf terminals. A woman on my team who did twenty years in the Coast Guard before she came to us. My boss ordered ten back in the spring, for his kids and the lake place, when all anybody else was buying was gas cans."

"What item."

"It's small. It's cheap, considering. It's no secret, you could look it up tonight. It's just that nobody outside my little world has tied it to any of this yet."

"Warren. What is it."

One more long look.

Then: "Stay put."

He went in his shop. Came back out with something in his hand.

Black tube. Maybe nine inches. About the size of a flashlight.

He held it up.

"This."

"A flashlight?"

"A water filter. A straw, they call it. You can drink through it straight out of a pond. Or it threads onto a regular water bottle, any standard one. Rain barrel. Creek. The bathtub you filled before the pressure dropped. No batteries. Nothing to plug in. One of these is good for 1,800 gallons."

"And that's what..."

"That's what we've all got. There's one in Marlene's glove box, she just doesn't know what it is. One in each of the girls' backpacks. That's the item."

"That little thing."

"That's why it works. Goes in a purse. Needs no power and no refills. And nobody can put it on a conservation order."

"Warren, does that thing actually work?"

"I'll let you answer that yourself in about five minutes. You got an empty water bottle in your recycling? Go get it."

I went and got one. Plain store water bottle out of the bin. Followed him around the back of his shop.

There's a rain barrel back there under the downspout. Been there since before we moved in. Nobody's cleaned it in years. Brown. Leaves rotting in the bottom. You wouldn't let a dog drink out of it.

He took the lid off.

Took my bottle.

Pushed it down under the surface and let it fill. It came up the color of old dishwater with bits turning over in it.

Then he threaded the straw on where the cap goes.

Handed it to me.

"Drink."

"Warren."

"Drink."

"You go first."

That got a real grin out of him. He took it back, tipped it up and drank a good third of it. Wiped his mouth on his sleeve.

Handed it over.

I looked at it for a while.

Then I drank.

I was braced for it to taste the way that barrel smells.

It tasted like nothing. Like the water out of my fridge door. No grit. No pond. No smell.

I held the bottle up to the light.

What was in the bottle was still brown.

What came through the straw was clear.

"Well, I'll be."

"That's all there is to it."

"And it does that with anything?"

"Anything fresh. It won't do the ocean, it can't take out salt. But a creek, a pond, a lake, rain water, a stock tank. The tub you filled."

"And what's it take out."

"There's two stages in there. A membrane that goes down to 0.01 micron. That's what stops bacteria and parasites, the stuff that puts you on the bathroom floor. Then a carbon stage for chemicals and sediment."

I stood there holding the bottle.

"Warren, where do you even get one."

"Same place everybody I work with got theirs. I'll write it down for you."

He unscrewed the straw and put it in my hand.

"Keep that one. I've got a case. I'll leave you some tomorrow. Give them to your kids. Tell them it's from their mother and she'll sleep better. Leave me out of it. They don't have to believe a word of this. They just have to have it in a drawer on the day."

"Warren."

"Forget the wood stove if you want. Forget the cash and every other thing I said. I wouldn't. But you could. This one you can't skip."

"All right."

"When the orders come and everybody's standing in a line for their allotment, the woman with one of these in her purse isn't standing in the water line. There's a word I keep landing on for that. Free. Whatever they shut off, it stops at the edge of that pond down the road for anybody who owns one of these."

"Most folks are going to hear about this on the six o'clock news. That's a week too late. You're hearing it from me, today, over a fence. Do something with it."

He went back to his wood pile.

I went inside. Put it in the junk drawer next to the batteries. Told myself Warren had sat in too many meetings.

I left it there two days.

Then I sat down with my iPad and started checking up on him.

Slovenia really did start rationing gas in March. First country in the EU to do it.

The Philippines really did declare a national energy emergency.

The head of the International Energy Agency called this "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." In April he went on CNBC and said "We are facing the biggest energy security threat in history."

Every single thing Warren said about the oil side checked out.

Then I looked up Texas. February 2021. 14.4 million people with their water disrupted. 190 counties.

Just like he said. Right down to the man with the eight chickens.

Warren left a grocery sack hanging on my back door handle the next morning. Didn't knock. Four more of them inside.

I called my daughter that afternoon and said I was coming over.

I gave her two. One for her kitchen, one for her husband's truck.

I drove to my son's and gave him two. One for the house, one for the diaper bag.

The one from the fence stayed in my junk drawer.

My son gave me the look. Same one he's been giving me since he was fifteen.

Doesn't bother me one bit.

If you've had a feeling for a while now that something is off, that the news keeps walking around something without ever saying it, you are not going crazy.

The people who deal with this for a living already took care of their own houses. Quietly. No announcement.

Warren had one thing dead right. By the time it's on the six o'clock news, the shelf is already bare. The person in the line is the person who heard last.

This is the same straw Warren handed me over the fence. I've put the link below.

I'm not a prepper. I'm a grandmother with a junk drawer. But when the orders come and the lines start, I'd like to be the woman who took care of it back in September.

👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial

EDITED:

On September 11th, drones hit that pipeline across Saudi Arabia and shut it down. The one that carries oil around the strait. Warren's side door. I'd written it on the back of an envelope the night he told me. I've still got the envelope.

On September 13th, eight ships went through the strait. Eight. It used to be about 85 a day. Another ship got hit that same day. Iran's parliament speaker says it "will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met." AAA said gas jumped 13 cents in a single week.

Then last Wednesday my phone rang before 6 in the morning. My sister, out in Wichita.

The main water plant there lost power around 5am. It was already running on backup generators because of a storm, and the generators quit. 45 minutes. That's all it was. The pressure dropped and about half a million people, roughly one out of every six people in the state of Kansas, got told to boil their water. Some of the elementary schools closed. The last of it wasn't cleared until Sunday afternoon.

She sent me a picture from her Dillons. The water aisle. Bare metal shelves.

No war in Kansas. No conservation order. A generator that didn't do its job for 45 minutes.

"The tap goes too." He said that to me not three weeks before my own sister was boiling water on the stove to make her coffee.

I made this post because I couldn't keep sitting on it. Not after Wichita.

Warren still leaves Monday and comes home Thursday. Marlene knows he isn't sick now. He finally sat her down and told her all of it. She says he's at the kitchen table at three most nights. I haven't asked what the meetings are about these days. I don't believe I want to know.

My sister ordered a 5-pack from that same kitchen while her water was still on boil. My daughter ordered one too, the night I sent her the Wichita story. My son hasn't ordered a thing. He did leave the one in the diaper bag though. I checked.

I went back on the site myself this morning and read every line of the fine print before I told one more person to spend money. Here's what I found. The 5-pack is the one they've got marked most popular, and it comes with a survival guide and 16 emergency checklists thrown in free. Shipping is free. And you get 365 days to change your mind. A full year. "No forms to fill out. No evidence required." Those are their words, I copied them down.

So if you've read this far and you're on the fence, you've got a year to decide I'm a silly old woman. I hope I am.

👉 https://www.tryblackoutwater.com/pages/advertorial

P.S. I finally told my husband. All of it, start to finish. Even the part about the sippy cup. He sat there and didn't say a word the whole time. When I was done he got up, went to the junk drawer, took out the one Warren gave me, walked it out to the garage and put it in the door pocket of his truck. Then he came back in and said two words. "Order more." I already had.

P.P.S. If you're wondering how many, here's how I worked it out. One for every person in the house. One for each car, because you won't be home when it happens, you'll be at the grocery or at church. One in the bag by the door. For the two of us that came to five, which is how they sell them anyway. My daughter's house needed five too. If you only get one, fine, get the one. But count heads first.

P.P.P.S. Each straw is good for 1,800 gallons. The government's own Ready.gov page says to figure a gallon per person per day. Do that math. That's years, from a creek or a pond or a rain barrel or the tub you filled ahead of time. 0.01 micron membrane plus a carbon stage, so it's bacteria, parasites, sediment and chemicals. No batteries. Nothing to charge. There's no expiry date on them either, the site says they'll keep in a drawer 10 years. Free shipping, and the 365 day money back guarantee I told you about. Warren wouldn't have hung a sack of them on my door and told me to hand them to my grandkids if they didn't work. That was enough for me.

P.P.P.P.S. If you're thinking you'll just stack up water in the garage instead, I did that too, and you should. But think about what Warren is doing with that wood pile. Wood burns down. So does stored water. Whatever you've got on those shelves, it's a number that only goes one direction. And when it hits zero the tap isn't safe and the truck isn't coming. The straw is a different kind of thing. As long as there's a pond or a creek or rain coming off a roof somewhere you can walk to, you have water you can drink. One runs out. The other one doesn't. Get the straw.
